'''Mangosteen''' ('''''Garcinia mangostana'''''), also called '''mangostan'''<ref name="Collins">{{Cite web |title=mangostan |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/mangostan |website=Collins English Dictionary |access-date=16 November 2025 |archive-date=30 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430092238/https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/mangostan |url-status=live }}</ref> or '''purple mangosteen''', is a tropical [[evergreen]] tree with edible fruit native to the [[Malay Peninsula]] and [[Borneo]]. It has been cultivated extensively in tropical Asia since ancient times.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="Yao">{{Cite journal |last1=Yao |first1=T. L. |last2=Nazre |first2=M. |last3=McKey |first3=D. |last4=Jalonen |first4=R. |last5=Duminil |first5=J. |date=March 2023 |title=The origin of cultivated mangosteen ( Garcinia mangostana L. var. mangostana ): Critical assessments and an evolutionary-ecological perspective |journal=Ecology and Evolution |volume=13 |issue=3 |article-number=e9792 |doi=10.1002/ece3.9792 |doi-access=free |pmc=10020034 |pmid=36937066|bibcode=2023EcoEv..13E9792Y }}</ref><ref name="Nazre-2014">{{Cite journal |last=Nazre |first=M. |date=August 2014 |title=New evidence on the origin of mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana L.) based on morphology and ITS sequence |journal=Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=1147–1158 |doi=10.1007/s10722-014-0097-2 |bibcode=2014GRCEv..61.1147N }}</ref><ref name="Morton-1987">{{Cite web |last=Morton |first=Julia F |year=1987 |title=Mangosteen |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/mangosteen.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140619231008/http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/mangosteen.html |archive-date=19 June 2014 |access-date=4 December 2012 |website=Fruits of warm climates |publisher=Purdue University |pages=301–304}}</ref> It is grown mainly in Southeast Asia, southwest India and other tropical areas such as Colombia, Puerto Rico and Florida,<ref name="Morton-1987" /><ref name="Karp-2006">{{Cite news |last=Karp |first=David |date=9 August 2006 |title=Forbidden? Not the Mangosteen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/09/dining/09mang.html?ex=1312776000&en=0d1a76f2087e406d&ei=5088&partner=rssnyt&emc=rss. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071017022402/http://nytimes.com/2006/08/09/dining/09mang.html?ex=1312776000&en=0d1a76f2087e406d&ei=5088&partner=rssnyt&emc=rss. |archive-date=17 October 2007 |access-date=22 May 2010 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name="Karp-2007">{{Cite news |last=Karp |first=David |date=8 August 2007 |title=Mangosteens Arrive, but Be Prepared to Pay |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/08/08/dining/08mang.html |access-date=22 May 2010 |work=The New York Times |archive-date=7 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207172556/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/08/08/dining/08mang.html |url-status=live }}</ref> where the tree has been introduced. The tree grows from {{convert|6|to|25|m|ft|1|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="Morton-1987"/>

The fruit of the mangosteen is sweet and tangy, juicy, somewhat fibrous, with fluid-filled vesicles and an inedible, deep reddish-purple colored rind ([[exocarp]]) when ripe.<ref name="Morton-1987" /><ref name="Karp-2006"/> The fragrant edible flesh that surrounds each seed is the [[endocarp]], i.e., the inner layer of the [[Ovary (plants)|ovary]].<ref name="Mabberley-1997">Mabberley, D.J. 1997. The plant book: A portable dictionary of the vascular plants. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=''Garcinia mangostana'' (Clusiaceae) |url=http://www.montosogardens.com/garcinia_mangostana.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090312024454/http://www.montosogardens.com/garcinia_mangostana.htm |archive-date=12 March 2009 |access-date=4 December 2012 |publisher=Montoso Gardens}}</ref> The seeds are of similar size and shape to almonds.

The genus ''[[Garcinia]]'' also contains several less-known fruit-bearing species, such as the [[button mangosteen]] (''G. prainiana'') and the [[charichuelo]] (''G. madruno'').

== Description ==
=== Tree ===
[[File:Pokok manggis.jpg|thumb|right|Mangosteen tree]]
[[File:Mangosteen Basket.jpg|thumb|Basket of fresh mangosteens]]
A tropical tree, the mangosteen must be grown in consistently warm conditions, as exposure to temperatures below {{convert|0|C|F}} for prolonged periods will usually kill a mature plant. They are known to recover from brief cold spells rather well, often with damage only to young growth. Experienced horticulturists have grown this species outdoors, and brought them to fruit in extreme south Florida.<ref name="Karp-2006"/>

The tree grows from {{convert|6|to|25|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} tall.<ref name="Morton-1987"/>

=== Fruit ===
The juvenile mangosteen fruit, which does not require fertilisation to form (see [[agamospermy]]), first appears as pale green or almost white in the shade of the [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]]. As the fruit enlarges over the next two to three months, the [[exocarp]] colour deepens to darker green. During this period, the fruit increases in size until its exocarp is {{convert|6|–|8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} in outside diameter, remaining hard until a final, abrupt ripening stage.<ref name="Crown-2014"/>

The subsurface chemistry of the mangosteen exocarp comprises an array of polyphenols, including [[xanthonoid|xanthones]] and [[tannin]]s that assure [[astringency]] which discourages infestation by insects, fungi, plant viruses, bacteria, and animal predation while the fruit is immature. Colour changes and softening of the exocarp are natural processes of ripening that indicate the fruit can be eaten and the seeds have finished developing.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 May 1996 |title=Plant Pigments for Color and Nutrition |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/midwest-area/madison-wi/vegetable-crops-research/docs/simon-pubs-97hort0012/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160629231946/http://www.ars.usda.gov/Research/docs.htm?docid=5383 |archive-date=29 June 2016 |access-date=26 November 2014 |publisher=US Department of Agriculture, republished from HortScience 32(1):12–13, 1997 |vauthors=Simon PW}}</ref>

Once the developing mangosteen fruit has stopped expanding, chlorophyll synthesis slows as the next colour phase begins. Initially streaked with red, the exocarp pigmentation transitions from green to red to dark purple, indicating a final ripening stage. This entire process takes place over a period of ten days as the edible quality of the fruit peaks. Over the days following removal from the tree, the exocarp hardens to an extent depending upon post-harvest handling and ambient storage conditions, especially relative humidity levels.  If the ambient humidity is high, exocarp hardening may take a week or longer when the flesh quality is peaking and excellent for consumption. However, after several additional days of storage, especially if unrefrigerated, the flesh inside the fruit might spoil without any obvious external indications. Using the hardness of the rind as an indicator of freshness for the first two weeks following harvest is therefore unreliable because the rind does not accurately reveal the interior condition of the flesh. If the exocarp is soft and yielding as it is when ripe and fresh from the tree, the fruit is usually good.<ref name="Crown-2014"/>

The edible endocarp of the mangosteen has the same shape and size as a tangerine {{convert|4|–|6|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} in diameter, but is white.<ref name="Crown-2014"/> The number of fruit segments corresponds exactly with the number of [[stigma (botany)|stigma]] lobes on the exterior [[apical meristem|apex]];<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Crown-2014"/> accordingly, a higher number of fleshy segments also corresponds with the fewest seeds.<ref name="Morton-1987"/> The circle of wedge-shaped segments contains 4–8, rarely 9 segments,<ref name="Crown-2014"/> the larger ones harbouring the [[apomictic]] seeds that are unpalatable unless roasted.<ref name="Morton-1987"/> As a non-[[climacteric (botany)|climacteric]] fruit, picked mangosteen does not ripen further, so it must be consumed shortly after harvest.<ref name=stone/><ref name="Crown-2014"/>

Often described as a subtle delicacy,<ref name=stone/><ref name="Crown-2014"/> the flesh bears an exceptionally mild aroma, quantitatively having about 1/400th of the chemical constituents of fragrant fruits, explaining its relative mildness.<ref name="MacLeod-1982">{{Cite journal |vauthors=MacLeod AJ, Pieris NM |year=1982 |title=Volatile flavour components of mangosteen, ''Garcinia mangostana'' |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.5555/19820304609 |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=117–9 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(82)80025-3|bibcode=1982PChem..21..117M |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The main volatile components having caramel, grass and butter notes as part of the mangosteen fragrance are [[hexyl acetate]], [[hexenol]] and α-[[copaene]].<ref name="MacLeod-1982"/> [[Ethyl octanoate]], [[ethyl hexanoate]] and [[Prenylthiol|3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol]] were detected as aroma components in mangosteen wine.<ref name="xiao">{{Cite journal |display-authors=3 |vauthors=Xiao ZB, Liu JH, Chen F, Wang LY, Niu YW, Feng T, Zhu JC |date=2015 |title=Comparison of aroma-active volatiles and their sensory characteristics of mangosteen wines prepared by Saccharomyces cerevisiae with GC-olfactometry and principal component analysis |journal=Natural Product Research |volume=29 |issue=7 |pages=656–62 |doi=10.1080/14786419.2014.981185 |pmid=25428208}}</ref>

==Origins and history==
Cultivated mangosteen (''Garcinia mangostana'' var. ''mangostana'') is [[dioecious]], but male trees are unknown. The trees produce viable seeds via [[apomixis]], where all the embryos are essentially clones of the mother.<ref name="Yao" /><ref name="Sobir">{{Cite journal |last1=Sobir |first1=Sobir |last2=Poerwanto |first2=Roedhy |last3=Santosa |first3=Edy |last4=Sinaga |first4=Soaloon |last5=Mansyah |first5=Elina |date=21 March 2011 |title=Genetic variability in apomictic mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) and its close relatives (Garcinia spp.) based on ISSR markers |journal=Biodiversitas Journal of Biological Diversity |volume=12 |issue=2 |doi=10.13057/biodiv/d120201|doi-access=free }}</ref> Its extensive cultivation has made its original native range difficult to ascertain. ''Garcinia mangostana'' var. ''mangostana'' is likely to be the domesticated descendant of wild populations of ''Garcinia mangostana'' var. ''malaccensis'' (previously thought to be a separate species) and''mangostana'' var. ''borneensis'', native to the Malay Peninsula and Borneo respectively. Both of these wild varieties still possess male trees, unlike the domesticated mangosteen. It may have also [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridized]] to a limited extent with closely related species, including ''Garcinia penangiana'' and ''Garcinia venulosa''.<ref name="Yao" /><ref name="Nazre2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Nazre |first1=M. |last2=Newman |first2=M. F. |last3=Pennington |first3=R. T. |last4=Middleton |first4=D. J. |date=23 October 2018 |title=Taxonomic Revision of Garcinia Section Garcinia (Clusiaceae) |journal=Phytotaxa |volume=373 |issue=1 |page=1 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.373.1.1 |bibcode=2018Phytx.373....1N |url=http://publication.plazi.org/id/F6787E35FFEB3B10FF9EC8245F20FFEB }}</ref>

Mangosteens are highly valued for their juicy, delicate texture and slightly sweet and sour flavor. The mangosteen has been cultivated in Malaysia,  Sri Lanka, Borneo, Sumatra, Mainland Southeast Asia, and the Philippines since ancient times. The 15th-century Chinese record [[Yingya Shenglan]] described mangosteen as ''mang-chi-shih'' (derived from Malay ''manggis''), a native plant of Southeast Asia of white flesh with a delectable sweet and sour taste.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ma |first1=Huan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DjQ9AAAAIAAJ |title=Ying-yai Sheng-lan: 'The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores' (1433) |last2=Feng |first2=Chengjun |last3=Mills |first3=John Vivian Gottlieb |date=2 December 1970 |publisher=CUP Archive |isbn=978-0-521-01032-0 |page=92 |access-date=2 May 2015}}</ref>

[[File:Flowers and fruit of the mangosteen, and Singapore monkey, by Marianne North.jpg|thumb|Flowers and fruit of the mangosteen, and Singapore monkey, by [[Marianne North]], before 1890]]

A description of mangosteen was included in the ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753. The mangosteen was introduced into English greenhouses in 1855.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mangosteen |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/362018/mangosteen |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527071705/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/362018/mangosteen |archive-date=27 May 2015 |access-date=2 May 2015 |publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica}}</ref> Subsequently, its culture was introduced into the Western Hemisphere, where it became established in West Indies islands, especially Jamaica. It was later established on the American mainland in Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, and Ecuador. The mangosteen tree generally does not grow well outside the tropics.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

In Southeast Asia, mangosteen is commonly known as the "Queen of Fruits", and is frequently paired with [[durian]], the "King of Fruits".<ref name="meridian">{{Cite magazine |url=http://meridian103.com/issue-7/flora-and-fauna/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220327071105/http://meridian103.com/issue-7/flora-and-fauna/ |archive-date=2022-03-27 |title=The King and Queen of Fruits: the Durian and Mangosteen|department=Flora and Fauna|magazine=103 Meridian East|issue=7|date=September 2010}}</ref> In [[Chinese food therapy]], mangosteen is considered "cooling", making it a good counterbalance to the "heaty" durian.<ref name="meridian" />  There is also a legend about [[Victoria of the United Kingdom|Queen Victoria]] offering a reward of one hundred [[pounds sterling]] to anyone who could deliver a fresh mangosteen to her.<ref name="Karp-2006"/><ref name="Crown-2014"/> Although this legend can be traced to a 1930 publication by the fruit explorer [[David Fairchild]],<ref name="stone">{{Cite web |last=Stone |first=Daniel |date=26 May 2016 |title=Meet the mangosteen |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/meet-the-mangosteen |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210226040552/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/meet-the-mangosteen |archive-date=26 February 2021 |access-date=14 Nov 2021 |website=The Plate |publisher=National Geographic}}</ref> it is not substantiated by any known historical document.<ref name="Crown-2014"/>

The journalist and gourmet [[R. W. Apple Jr.]] once said of the fruit, "No other fruit, for me, is so thrillingly, intoxicatingly luscious...I'd rather eat one than a hot fudge sundae, which for a big Ohio boy is saying a lot."<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 Sep 2003 |title=Forbidden Fruit: Something About A Mangosteen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/09/24/dining/forbidden-fruit-something-about-a-mangosteen.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131010084938/http://www.nytimes.com/2003/09/24/dining/forbidden-fruit-something-about-a-mangosteen.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm |archive-date=10 October 2013 |access-date=13 June 2012 |work=New York Times |vauthors=Apple RW}}</ref>  Since 2006, private small-volume orders for fruits grown in Puerto Rico have been sold to American specialty food stores and gourmet restaurants who serve the flesh segments as a delicacy dessert.<ref name=stone/><ref name="Karp-2006" />

==Propagation, cultivation and harvest==
Mangosteen is usually propagated by seedlings.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006">{{Cite book |last=bin Osman |first=Mohamad |title=Mangosteen Garcinia mangostana L. |date=2006 |publisher=University of Southampton |isbn=0-85432-817-3 |location=Southampton, UK}}</ref> [[Vegetative propagation]] is difficult and seedlings are more robust and reach fruiting earlier than vegetatively propagated plants.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/>

Mangosteen produces a [[recalcitrant seed]] which is not a true seed strictly defined, but rather described as a [[nucellar]] [[asexual reproduction|asexual]] [[embryo]].<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Crown-2014">{{Cite web |date=2014 |title=Science: Mangosteen information |url=http://mangosteen.com/Sciencenonscienceandnonsense.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070429041504/http://www.mangosteen.com/Sciencenonscienceandnonsense.htm |archive-date=29 April 2007 |access-date=2 May 2007 |website=Mangosteen.com |publisher=The mangosteen website |vauthors=Crown I}}</ref><ref name="Osman-2006"/> As seed formation involves no sexual fertilization, the seedling is genetically identical to the mother plant.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/> If allowed to dry, a seed dies quickly, but if soaked, seed germination takes between 14 and 21 days when the plant can be kept in a nursery for about 2 years growing in a small pot.<ref name="Osman-2006"/>

When the trees are approximately {{convert|25|-|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}, they are transplanted to the field at a spacing of {{convert|20|-|40|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/>  After planting, the field is mulched in order to control weeds.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Yaacob">{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/mangosteencultiv00othm |title=Mangosteen cultivation |vauthors=Yaacob O, Tindall HD |date=1995 |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations |isbn=92-5-103459-1 |location=Rome}}</ref> Transplanting takes place in the rainy season because young trees are likely to be damaged by drought.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/> Because young trees need shade,<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name= Yaacob/> [[intercropping]] with banana, [[true plantain|plantain]], [[rambutan]], [[durian]] or coconut leaves is effective.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/>  Coconut palms are mainly used in areas with a long dry season, as palms also provide shade for mature mangosteen trees.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/> Another advantage of intercropping in mangosteen cultivation is the suppression of weeds.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name= Yaacob/>

The growth of the trees is slowed if the temperature is below {{convert|20|C}}. The ideal temperature range for growing and producing fruits is {{convert|25-35|C}}<ref name="Diczbalis-2011">{{Cite journal |last=Diczbalis |first=Yan |date=2011 |title=Farm and Forestry Production and Marketing for Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) |journal=Elevitch C.R.}}</ref> with relative humidity over 80%.<ref name= Yaacob/> The maximal temperature is {{convert|38-40|C}}, with both leaves and fruit being susceptible to scorching and sunburn,<ref name= Yaacob/><ref name="Diczbalis-2011"/> while the minimum temperature is {{convert|3-5|C}}.<ref name="Diczbalis-2011"/> Young seedlings prefer a high level of shade and mature trees are shade-tolerant.<ref name="Diczbalis-2011"/>

Mangosteen trees have a weak root system and prefer deep, well-drained soils with high moisture content, often growing on riverbanks.<ref name= Yaacob/> The mangosteen is not adapted to limestone soils, [[alluvial]] soils, or sandy soils with low organic matter content.<ref name="Diczbalis-2011"/><ref name="Paull-2012">{{Cite book |title=Mangosteen |vauthors=Paull RE, Duarte O |date=2012 |publisher=Crop Production Science in Horticulture}}</ref> Mangosteen trees need a well-distributed rainfall over the year (<40 mm/month) and a 3–5 week dry season.<ref name="Diczbalis-2011"/>

Mangosteen trees are sensitive to water availability and application of fertilizer input which is increased with the age of trees, regardless of region.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name= Yaacob/> Maturation of mangosteen fruits takes 5–6 months, with harvest occurring when the [[pericarp]]s are purple.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Crown-2014"/>

===Breeding===
In the breeding of [[perennial]] mangosteen, the selection of rootstock and grafting are significant issues to overcome constraints to production, harvesting, or seasonality.<ref name="Morton-1987"/> Most of the [[genetic resources]] for breeding are in [[germplasm]] collections, whereas some wild species are cultivated in Malaysia and the Philippines.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Osman-2006"/> Conservation methods are chosen because storage of seeds under dried and low-temperature conditions has not been successful.<ref name="Morton-1987"/>

Because of the long duration until the trees yield fruits and the long resulting breeding cycles, mangosteen breeding has not proven attractive for transplanting or research.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Te-chato">{{Cite book |last1=Te-chato |first1=Sompong |title=Biotechnology of Fruit and Nut Crops |last2=Lim |first2=Mongkol |publisher=CABI Publishing |year=2005 |editor-last=Litz |editor-first=R. E. |location=Wallingford, UK |chapter=7.1 Garcinia mangostana Mangosteen}}</ref> Breeding objectives that may enhance mangosteen production include:<ref name= Te-chato/>
* Drought tolerance, especially sensitivity to drought in the first 5 years after germination
* Tree architecture to produce a tree with a crown that is regular and pyramid-shaped
* Fruit quality including i) overcoming bitter taste components caused by changes in pulp, [[pericarp]] or [[aril]] and ii) pericarp cracking resulting from excessive water uptake
* [[Rootstock]] for improved adaptation to drought and robust development in early years of growth

===Yield===
Mangosteen trees may reach fruit-bearing in as little as 6 years but may require 12 or more years, depending on climate and cultivation methods.<ref name="Morton-1987"/> The yield of the mangosteen is variable, depending on the climate and age of the tree.<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Crown-2014"/> If the young tree is bearing for the first time, 200–300 fruits may be produced, whereas at maturity, 500 fruits per season are average.<ref name="Morton-1987"/> At age 30 to 45 years in full maturity, each tree may yield as many as 3,000 fruits, with trees as old as 100 years still producing.<ref name="Morton-1987"/>

===Regional production===
Major mangosteen production occurs in Southeast Asia, mainly in Thailand as the country with the most acreage planted, estimated at 4,000 ha in 1965<ref name="Morton-1987"/> and 11,000 ha in 2000, giving a total yield of 46,000 tons.<ref name="Osman-2006"/> Mangosteen is seasonally available in Thailand from May through September.{{cn|date=August 2025}} Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines are other major Asian producers.<ref name="Osman-2006"/>  Mangosteen production in Colombia and Puerto Rico has been successful.<ref name=stone/><ref name="Karp-2006"/><ref name="Crown-2014"/>

===Diseases and pests===
====Common diseases and pests====

The [[pathogens]] that attack mangosteen are common in other tropical trees. The diseases can be divided into [[foliar]], fruit, stem and soil-borne diseases.<ref name="Lim-2003">{{Cite book |title=Diseases of Tropical Fruit Crops |vauthors=Lim TK, Sangchote S |publisher=CABI Publishing |year=2003 |veditors=Ploetz RC |location=Wallingford, UK |chapter=16 Diseases on Mangosteen}}</ref>

[[Pestalotiopsis]] leaf blight (''Pestalotiopsis flagisettula'', only identified in Thailand) is one of the diseases that infect especially young leaves.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> Furthermore, the pathogen causes the fruits to rot before and after the harvest.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> Additional [[stem canker]] and dieback are caused by the pathogen.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> Some of the symptoms of stem canker are branch splitting, [[gummosis]] and bark blistering.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> The main areas where the disease was observed are Thailand, Malaysia, and [[North Queensland]].<ref name="Lim-2003"/>

Another common disease is the thread blight or white thread blight disease (''[[Marasmiellus scandens]]'') whereas the name comes from the [[mycelia]] which resembles thread.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> Leaves, twigs, and branches may also be damaged by the disease.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> The [[spores]] spread with the help of wind, raindrops, and insects, and thrive in shady, humid, and wet conditions.<ref name="Lim-2003"/>

An important post-harvest disease affecting mangosteen, especially in Thailand is called Diplodia fruit rot (''[[Diplodia theobromae]]'') which, as a secondary pathogen, enters the host plant through wounds.<ref name="Lim-2003"/>

''[[Phellinus noxius]]'' living on the roots and trunk bases causes brown root disease, a name derived from the appearance of the [[mycelium]]-binding soil particles.<ref name="Lim-2003"/> The distribution of the fungus happens through contact with infected wood or thick [[rhizomorphs]] on tree stumps.<ref name="Lim-2003"/>

There are a few pests that feed on mangosteen leaves and fruits including [[leaf eater]] (''[[Stictoptera]]'' sp.), [[leaf miner]] (''Phyllocnictis citrella'') and fruit borer (''[[Curculio]]'' sp.).<ref name="Osman-2006"/> Especially in nurseries, the [[larval stage]] of the leaf eater can cause visible damage on young leaves, but can be managed by biological control agents.<ref name="Osman-2006"/> The larval stage of fruit borer (''Curculio'' sp.) feeds on different parts of fruit before ripening.<ref name="Osman-2006"/>

====Control measures for diseases and pests====
Different management options can be applied to control mangosteen diseases.<ref name="Osman-2006"/><ref name="Lim-2003"/>
* Measures to inhibit sun scalding to minimize leaf blight and stem canker.
* Reduction of wounds caused by insects and storm damage to minimize disease incidence.
* Change of the [[microclimate]] by tree spacing and pruning.
* Chemicals applied to root collars and tree stumps to control root diseases.
* Fungicides to control fungal pathogens.
* [[Biological pest control]] or insecticides to control insects.

==Uses==
[[File:Young Mangosteen Fruit.jpg|thumb|right|Young fruit]]

===Culinary===
Without [[fumigation]] or [[irradiation]] to kill the Asian [[Tephritidae|fruit fly]], fresh mangosteens were illegal to import into the United States until 2007.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Karp |first=David |date=27 June 2007 |title=Welcome at the border: Thai fruits, once banned |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/27/dining/27frui.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240821051123/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/27/dining/27frui.html |archive-date=21 August 2024 |access-date=22 May 2010 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Following export from its natural growing regions in Southeast Asia (particularly Thailand), the fresh fruit is available seasonally in some local markets in North America such as those of [[Chinatown]]s.<ref name="Karp-2006"/><ref name="Beech-2020"/> Mangosteens are available fresh, canned and frozen in Western countries. The fruit may be served as a dessert or made into jams.<ref name="Crown-2014"/> In Vietnam, the ripe fruit is also used as a salad ingredient.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 1, 2017 |title=Mangosteen salad |url=https://eng.binhduong.gov.vn/dautuphattrien/Lists/UsefulInformation/DispForm.aspx?ID=86&CategoryId=Cuisine |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240821051136/https://eng.binhduong.gov.vn/dautuphattrien/Lists/UsefulInformation/DispForm.aspx?ID=86&CategoryId=Cuisine |archive-date=21 August 2024 |access-date=April 9, 2019 |publisher=Binh Duong Government}}</ref>

Upon arrival in the US in 2007, fresh mangosteens sold at up to {{convert|60|$/lb|$/kg|order=flip|abbr=on}} in specialty produce stores in New York City, but wider availability and somewhat lower prices have become common in the United States and Canada.<ref name="Karp-2007"/><ref name="Beech-2020">{{Cite news |last=Hannah Beech |date=2020-06-22 |title=Eating Thai fruit demands serious effort but delivers sublime reward |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/22/world/asia/bangkok-thailand-fruit-durian.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200629224847/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/22/world/asia/bangkok-thailand-fruit-durian.html |archive-date=29 June 2020 |access-date=2020-06-29 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Despite efforts described above to grow mangosteen in the Western Hemisphere, nearly the entire supply is imported from Thailand.<ref name="faothai">{{Cite web |title=Market Potential for Mangosteen and Salaaca |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/meeting/022/ma800E.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924134938/http://www.fao.org/docrep/meeting/022/ma800E.pdf |archive-date=24 September 2015 |access-date=December 4, 2014 |publisher=Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations}}</ref>

Before ripening, the mangosteen shell is fibrous and firm but becomes soft and easy to pry open when the fruit ripens. To open a mangosteen, the shell can be scored with a knife, pried gently along the score with the thumbs until it cracks, and then pulled apart to reveal the fruit.<ref name="Crown-2014"/> Alternatively, the mangosteen can be opened without a knife by squeezing the shell from the bottom until it breaks, allowing the shell to be removed and the fruit eaten while intact with the stem.<ref name="withhands">{{Cite web |date=2014 |title=How To Open A Mangosteen |url=http://www.thailandbreeze.com/how-to-open-a-mangosteen.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240821051127/http://www.thailandbreeze.com/how-to-open-a-mangosteen.html |archive-date=21 August 2024 |access-date=March 11, 2017 |publisher=Thailand Breeze}}</ref> In Southeast Asian countries, the mangosteen is usually served with the bottom part of the shell intact.<ref name="serve">{{Cite web |date=2023 |title=How to open a mangosteen properly |url=https://www.thaisolutions1502.com/mangosteen/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240106023941/https://www.thaisolutions1502.com/mangosteen/ |archive-date=6 January 2024 |access-date=January 5, 2023 |publisher=Thai Solutions}}</ref> Occasionally, during peeling of ripe fruits, the purple exocarp juice may stain skin or fabric.<ref name="Crown-2014"/>

===Traditional medicine===
Various parts of the plant have a history of use in traditional medicine, mostly in Southeast Asia; it may have been used to treat skin infections, wounds, dysentery, urinary tract infections, and gastrointestinal complaints,<ref name="Morton-1987"/><ref name="Obolskiy-2009">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Obolskiy D, Pischel I, Siriwatanametanon N, Heinrich M |date=August 2009 |title=Garcinia mangostana L.: a phytochemical and pharmacological review |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=23 |issue=8 |pages=1047–65 |doi=10.1002/ptr.2730 |pmid=19172667 |s2cid=23701150}}</ref> although there is no high-quality clinical evidence for any of these effects.<ref name="Gross-2009"/>

Dried fruits are shipped to Singapore to be processed for medical uses which may include dysentery, skin disorders, and various other minor diseases in several countries across Asia.<ref name="Morton-1987" /> There is no reliable evidence that mangosteen juice, puree, bark or extracts is effective as a treatment for human diseases.<ref name="Gross-2009">{{Cite web |date=May 21, 2009 |title=The Mangosteen Controversy |url=http://newhope360.com/supplements/mangosteen-controversy |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103034303/http://newhope360.com/supplements/mangosteen-controversy |archive-date=3 November 2013 |access-date=4 January 2010 |website=New Hope Network |vauthors=Gross P, Crown I}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2016 |title=Mangosteen uses |url=http://www.webmd.com/vitamins-supplements/ingredientmono-1081-mangosteen.aspx?activeingredientid=1081&activeingredientname=mangosteen |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170507104227/http://www.webmd.com/vitamins-supplements/ingredientmono-1081-mangosteen.aspx?activeingredientid=1081&activeingredientname=mangosteen |archive-date=7 May 2017 |access-date=18 September 2016 |website=WebMD}}</ref>

The extract of mangosteen peels is traditionally used in Indonesia as natural dye for coloring tenun [[ikat]] and [[batik]] textiles in brown, dark brown, purple or red hues.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kusumawati |first1=Nita |last2=Santoso |first2=Agus Budi |last3=Sianita |first3=Maria Monica |last4=Muslim |first4=Supari |year=2017 |title=Extraction, Characterization and Application of Natural Dyes from the Fresh Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana L.) Peel |journal=International Journal on Advanced Science, Engineering and Information Technology |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |page=878 |doi=10.18517/ijaseit.7.3.1014 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The mangosteen's lobed [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] ({{lang|ms|tampuk manggis}}) is a common pattern in Malay fabrics like the [[songket]],<ref>{{cite book |author=Haziyah Hussin<!-- xct nm --> |year=2010 |title=Nature Motifs in Malay Batik and Songket |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5bnHLnfDxekC&q=tampuk+mangosteen |location=Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia |publisher=Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka |page=146 |isbn=978-983-46-0575-9 }}</ref> it symbolises one's pleasant character regardless of their appearance.<ref>{{cite book |author=Arba'iyah Abdul Aziz |date=2018 |title=Simbolisme Dalam Motif Songket Melayu Terengganu |location=Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia |publisher=Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka |page=103 |isbn=978-983-46-1686-1}}</ref>

===Other uses===
Mangosteen twigs have been used as chew sticks in Ghana, and the wood has been used to make spears and cabinetry in Thailand. The rind of the mangosteen fruit has also been used to tan leather in China.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

==Phytochemicals==
Mangosteen peel contains [[xanthonoids]], such as [[mangostin]], and other [[phytochemicals]].<ref name="Obolskiy-2009"/>
[[Polysaccharide]] and [[xanthone]] compounds are found in the fruit, leaves, and heartwood of the mangosteen.<ref name="Obolskiy-2009"/> Fully ripe fruit contain the xanthones {{ndash}} gartanin, 8-disoxygartanin, and normangostin.<ref name="Morton-1987" />

==Marketing==
Fresh mangosteen is marketed for only a short period of six to ten weeks due to its seasonal nature.<ref name="Karp-2007"/><ref name="Osman-2006" /> It is mainly grown by [[smallholder]]s and sold at fruit stalls by roadsides. Its irregular, short supply leads to wide price fluctuations throughout its season and over the years.<ref name="Karp-2006"/><ref>{{Cite web |date=31 July 2007 |title=Mangosteen price too low: farmers |url=http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/07/31/national/national_30043072.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120921231512/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/07/31/national/national_30043072.php |archive-date=21 September 2012 |access-date=4 December 2012 |publisher=The Nation}}</ref>  Additionally, there is no standard product quality assessment or grading system, making international trade of the fruit difficult.<ref name="Osman-2006"/>  The mangosteen still remains rare in Western markets, though its popularity is increasing, and it is often sold at a high price.<ref name="Karp-2007"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Temple-West |first=Patrick |date=5 March 2008 |title=Tropical sweetness: harnessing the elusive mangosteen |url=http://news.medill.northwestern.edu/washington/news.aspx?id=80519 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100110014929/http://news.medill.northwestern.edu/washington/news.aspx?id=80519 |archive-date=10 January 2010 |access-date=4 December 2012 |publisher=Medill Reports}}</ref>
